claims.text: A blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ and covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK tied infrastructure to AWS.
Multi-cloud was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
With CDK and CloudFormation, the infrastructure code acts as a code generator producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources.
AWS CDK is AWS-only, while Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-prem.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python, while Pulumi supports any programming language.
AWS CDK deployments are slower due to CloudFormation, while Pulumi is faster due to direct execution.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file, while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK supports only AWS Secrets Manager for secrets management, while Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging while CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows for extensibility.
Pulumi executes infrastructure code directly during deployment rather than generating an intermediary format.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
Pulumi Insights product page provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
With CDK/CloudFormation, SST often had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to achieve desired functionality.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments documentation exists at /docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/ describing advanced deployment workflows.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies "day one" tasks, documented in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
An on-demand Pulumi workshop titled "Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" exists at the given resources URL.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications; its constructs/components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
SST is a framework for building modern full-stack applications on your own infrastructure.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` needs no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account, not in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of the SST framework.
The SST team has repeatedly said, since the rewrite shipped, that SST is built on the Pulumi engine architecture.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can deploy applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST users define app infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST components, and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported SST architecture since.

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs ('What is SST') say: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis' says SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to be defined and deployed.

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article 'SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion' says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published package.json for SST's platform package depends on @pulumi/pulumi, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider.

The anomalyco/sst repository (formerly sst/sst) has platform/package.json listing @pulumi/pulumi, @pulumi/aws, @pulumi/cloudflare, @pulumi/command, @pulumi/docker-build, @pulumi/random, @pulumi/tls, and @pulumiverse/vercel as direct dependencies.

In SST's deploy chain, SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs actual state, builds a dependency graph and orders operations, and Terraform-bridged providers translate resources into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's engine handles dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and provider API plumbing for hundreds of provider APIs in SST.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem with the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API works by embedding Pulumi programs inside other tools, and the same provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework whose docs state "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its Pulumi provider is described as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`".
Nitric and Defang, like SST, run application deployments through the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer.
SST does not require a Pulumi account; most SST users never write Pulumi code; users can define raw Pulumi resources inside an SST app and deploy them together with SST components.
SST's components are defined using Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine; SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has a larger following on GitHub (more stars) than SST itself.
opencode has grown quickly since launch.
SST's release cadence and its dependency on the Pulumi engine have not changed as a result of the team's work on opencode.
If you run SST, you are running Pulumi's engine.
Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, and components are available to teams whose needs grow past a single SST app, and none of them require leaving the engine SST already uses.
SST does not expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application on its own.
SST's abstractions are enough for a lot of teams and applications; SST is a strong fit for an opinionated full-stack application framework.
The blog post /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ exists and tells the story of SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
